title: High blood pressure (hypertension)
what: High blood pressure means the force of blood against your artery walls is consistently higher than it should be. Over time it can strain the heart, blood vessels, brain and kidneys. Many people have it without knowing, which is why regular checks matter.
symptoms: Most people have no symptoms at all.
Very high blood pressure can cause headaches, dizziness, blurred vision or nosebleeds.
Chest pain, shortness of breath or confusion can signal a serious problem that needs urgent care.
causes: Older age and a family history of high blood pressure
Eating a lot of salt and few fruits and vegetables
Being overweight or physically inactive
Tobacco use and harmful alcohol use
Long-term stress and some other health conditions
prevention: Have your blood pressure checked regularly, especially if you are over 40 or it runs in your family.
Cut down on salt in cooking and on heavily salted foods.
Eat more fruit, vegetables and whole foods.
Stay physically active on most days.
Avoid tobacco and limit alcohol.
If you have been prescribed medicine, take it as directed and keep review appointments.
seek: You have not had your blood pressure checked in the past year.
A previous reading was high.
You have diabetes or kidney problems, or heart disease or stroke runs in your family.
urgent: Sudden weakness or numbness, a drooping face, slurred speech or confusion
A very severe headache with vision changes

title: Diabetes awareness
what: Diabetes is a long-term condition in which the body cannot properly control the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood. Type 2 diabetes is the most common form and is linked to weight, activity and age. Type 1 diabetes usually starts earlier in life and needs insulin.
symptoms: Feeling very thirsty and passing urine more often.
Tiredness and blurred vision.
Losing weight without trying.
Cuts or sores that heal slowly, or frequent infections.
Some people have no symptoms at first.
causes: Being overweight, especially around the waist
Physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet
A family history of diabetes
Older age
High blood sugar during a previous pregnancy
prevention: Keep a healthy weight.
Be physically active. WHO advises adults to aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
Choose a healthy diet with less sugar, salt and saturated fat.
Avoid tobacco.
Ask about blood sugar testing if you have risk factors.
If you have diabetes, attend regular reviews and look after your feet.
seek: You have symptoms such as extreme thirst, frequent urination and unexplained weight loss.
You have risk factors and have never been tested.
You are pregnant and worried about your blood sugar.
urgent: Vomiting, stomach pain, fast or deep breathing, or a fruity smell on the breath
In a person with diabetes: sweating, shaking and confusion, which can mean low blood sugar

title: Malaria: prevention and when to get tested
what: Malaria is an illness spread by the bites of infected mosquitoes. It can be treated when found early, but it can become life-threatening if care is delayed. Risk differs between regions and seasons, and local health workers can advise on risk in your area.
symptoms: Fever and chills.
Headache and sweating.
Muscle aches and tiredness.
Nausea and vomiting.
causes: Living in or travelling to an area where malaria occurs
Mosquito bites, especially at dusk and dawn
Standing water near the home where mosquitoes breed
Pregnancy and early childhood, when illness can be more severe
prevention: Sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net.
Use a repellent suitable for your age and cover your skin at dusk and dawn.
Clear standing water around your home.
Follow Ministry of Health guidance on prevention, including for pregnant women and young children.
If you are travelling to a high-risk area, ask a health professional about preventive medicine before you go.
seek: You have a fever in an area where malaria occurs. Early testing and treatment matter.
A pregnant woman or young child has a fever.
You develop a fever after travel to a malaria area.
urgent: Severe weakness, being unable to sit or stand
Repeated vomiting or being unable to keep fluids down
Yellowing of the skin or eyes

title: Healthy ageing
what: Healthy ageing is about staying as independent, active and connected as possible as we get older. Small, regular habits make a real difference.
symptoms: Reduced strength and balance.
Changes in vision and hearing.
Changes in sleep.
Slower recovery from illness.
Mild forgetfulness is common, but sudden or marked confusion is not a normal part of ageing.
prevention: Stay active, including exercises for strength and balance.
Eat a varied diet and drink enough fluids.
Stay in touch with family, friends and community.
Keep long-term conditions under review and take medicines as directed.
Have vision and hearing checked.
Ask about vaccinations and screening that suit your age and health.
seek: Unexplained weight loss or loss of appetite.
Increasing forgetfulness or confusion.
Low mood or loneliness that does not lift.
Falls, or fear of falling.
Difficulty managing daily tasks or medicines.
urgent: Sudden weakness, a drooping face or difficulty speaking
A fall with a head injury, severe pain or being unable to move
refs: WHO: Ageing and health fact sheet

title: Fall prevention for older adults
what: A fall is when a person unintentionally comes to rest on the ground or a lower level. Falls are common in older adults and can cause serious injury, but many falls can be prevented.
symptoms_title: Signs someone may be at risk
symptoms: Unsteady walking, or holding onto furniture to get around.
A previous fall.
Fear of falling, or doing less because of it.
Dizziness on standing up.
causes: Muscle weakness and poor balance
Some medicines, or taking several at once
Poor lighting, loose rugs, slippery floors and stairs
Poor vision or unsuitable footwear
Dizziness, long-term conditions or a drop in blood pressure on standing
prevention: Do exercises that build strength and balance, as advised by a health professional.
Remove trip hazards, improve lighting and add handrails and non-slip mats.
Wear well-fitting shoes with good grip.
Have vision and hearing checked.
Ask for a review of medicines.
Stand up slowly after lying or sitting.
seek: After any fall, even if you feel unhurt.
Fear of falling is limiting what you do.
You notice new dizziness or unsteadiness.
urgent: A head injury, especially with drowsiness, vomiting or confusion
Severe pain or being unable to move or put weight on a limb

title: Maternal health
what: Maternal health covers the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth and after birth. Regular antenatal care, skilled care at birth and checks after delivery help protect both mother and baby.
symptoms: Nausea and tiredness, especially early on.
Backache and mild swelling of the feet and ankles.
Changes in appetite and mood.
Always mention any worry to a health worker.
causes: Pregnancy at a very young age or later in life
Existing conditions such as high blood pressure or diabetes
Complications in an earlier pregnancy
Anaemia or poor nutrition
Not being able to attend antenatal care
prevention: Start antenatal care early. WHO recommends at least eight contacts with health services during pregnancy.
Eat a varied diet and ask about iron and folic acid supplements.
Sleep under an insecticide-treated net in areas where malaria occurs.
Avoid tobacco and alcohol.
Plan the birth with a skilled health worker.
Attend check-ups after the birth.
seek: As soon as you think you may be pregnant.
If you have missed antenatal visits.
If you are worried about your baby's movements or any symptom.
urgent: The baby moving much less than usual
After birth: heavy bleeding, fever or foul-smelling discharge
refs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience

title: Child health and vaccination
what: A healthy childhood relies on good nutrition, protection from infection through vaccination, safe surroundings and quick care when a child is unwell.
symptoms: Colds, coughs and mild fevers.
Diarrhoea and vomiting.
Ear and skin infections.
Malaria, in areas where it occurs.
prevention: Follow the national immunisation schedule and keep your child's health booklet safe.
Breastfeed. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months.
From six months, add safe, nutritious foods alongside breastfeeding.
Wash hands and use safe drinking water.
Use an insecticide-treated net in areas where malaria occurs.
Keep medicines and cleaning products out of reach.
seek: You are worried about a child's fever or feeding.
Diarrhoea lasts several days or comes with signs of dehydration, such as very thirsty, sunken eyes or little urine.
A vaccine has been missed. Ask what catch-up is advised.
urgent: Very sleepy, hard to wake or floppy
A fever in a young baby
refs: WHO: Infant and young child feeding

title: Medication safety
what: Medicines help most when they are used correctly. The wrong medicine, the wrong amount or an unsafe combination can cause serious harm.
symptoms: A rash, itching or swelling after starting a medicine.
Unusual drowsiness, dizziness or stomach upset.
New symptoms soon after starting or changing a medicine.
causes: Not understanding the label or instructions
Sharing medicines or using someone else's
Using medicines that are out of date or poorly stored
Taking several medicines, including herbal ones, without telling your provider
Stopping or changing a dose without advice
prevention: Keep an up-to-date list of everything you take, including herbal and over-the-counter products.
Ask your prescriber or pharmacist what each medicine is for and how to take it.
Take medicines exactly as directed.
Never share prescription medicines.
Store medicines as the label says and out of children's reach.
Check expiry dates and ask how to dispose of unused medicines.
seek: A side effect worries you.
You often miss doses.
You are unsure whether medicines are safe together, or in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
urgent: Swelling of the lips, face or tongue, difficulty breathing or a widespread rash, which can be a severe allergic reaction
Suspected overdose, or a child or adult who has swallowed medicine not meant for them
Fainting or a seizure after taking a medicine

title: Common respiratory illnesses
what: Respiratory illnesses affect the nose, throat, airways and lungs. Many, such as the common cold, are mild and pass on their own. Others, such as pneumonia and tuberculosis (TB), need medical care.
symptoms: Cough, sore throat, runny or blocked nose.
Fever, aches and tiredness.
Fast or noisy breathing, or wheezing.
Chest pain when breathing or coughing.
A cough lasting more than two weeks, especially with fever, night sweats or weight loss, can be a sign of TB and needs assessment.
causes: Close contact with someone who is infected
Tobacco smoke and smoke from indoor cooking fires
Air pollution
Young children, older adults and people with long-term conditions or weakened immunity
Crowded or poorly ventilated spaces
prevention: Wash hands often.
Cover coughs and sneezes.
Keep children's vaccinations up to date.
Improve ventilation and avoid indoor smoke.
Avoid tobacco.
Stay at home when unwell where you can.
seek: A cough lasts more than two weeks.
A fever lasts more than a few days.
You have wheezing or breathlessness.
A child has a cough with fast breathing.
urgent: Difficulty breathing, or being unable to speak in full sentences
In a child: fast breathing, the chest pulling in, or being unable to drink
